title: One model server and a streaming gateway
goal: Serve a real open-weights model (Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct) with llama.cpp in Docker, put a TypeScript gateway in front of it that speaks the OpenAI Chat Completions API with SSE streaming, and log TTFT and TPOT for every request.

changes.note: Downloads the GGUF model pinned to a Hugging Face commit and verifies its SHA-256.
llama.cpp server b6075: 8,192-token context shared by 4 parallel slots, Prometheus metrics on.
node:http server: routes, readiness against the model server, graceful shutdown.
The request path: validate, stream from llama.cpp, re-emit SSE, measure, log. Cancels upstream when the client leaves.
fetch + a small SSE parser over llama.cpp's /v1/chat/completions.
Request validation and the OpenAI wire types.
StreamTimer: TTFT, TPOT and total time.
JSON body reading with a size limit; OpenAI-shaped errors.
One JSON object per log line.
No runtime dependencies yet: Node 22's fetch and http are enough.
Strict TypeScript compiled to CommonJS (stage 8 needs require hooks).

run.label: Start llama.cpp
run.cmd: docker compose up -d && docker compose ps

run.label: Install and start the gateway on your machine

verify.label: The model server is up
verify.expect: {"status":"ok"} (while the model loads you get HTTP 503 with a loading message; wait a few seconds)

verify.label: Stream a completion
verify.expect: One line per token, each 'data: {"choices":[{"index":0,"delta":{"content":"..."}...' arriving one after another, then a chunk with "choices":[] and a "usage" object, then 'data: [DONE]'. The words themselves vary.

verify.label: TTFT from the outside
verify.cmd: curl -s -o /dev/null -w 'ttfb=%{time_starttransfer}s total=%{time_total}s\n' localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Count from 1 to 20."}],"stream":true,"max_tokens":80}'
verify.expect: ttfb=... total=... with ttfb much smaller than total. The gateway sends headers with the first token, so ttfb is the TTFT a client sees.

verify.label: TTFT and TPOT in the gateway log
verify.cmd: (look at the npm run dev terminal)
verify.expect: {"event":"completion",...,"ttftMs":...,"tpotMs":...,"totalMs":...,"prefillTokens":...} for every request. Write down your TTFT and TPOT: they are your laptop's baseline.

verify.label: Cancellation reaches the model
verify.expect: curl stops after 1 second; the gateway logs {"event":"completion_cancelled","reason":"client disconnected",...} and `docker compose logs llm-1` shows the slot released early instead of generating all 400 tokens.

concepts.how: TTFT is dominated by prefill (compute-bound), TPOT by decode (bandwidth-bound); you now measure both.
Streaming, the KV cache per slot (--ctx-size split across --parallel) and the TTFT/TPOT definitions come straight from this lesson.
SSE instead of WebSockets: one-way server-to-client tokens over plain HTTP, which every proxy and client library already handles.
SSE rides on a long HTTP/1.1 response; under HTTP/2 many streams share one connection, which matters for browsers with many open chats.
Wire compatibility with an existing API (OpenAI's) is an API design choice: every client library works by changing one base URL.
End-to-end ≈ TTFT + (tokens − 1) × TPOT: latency and throughput per user are two different numbers.

checkpoints.text: llama.cpp answers /health and the gateway streams tokens with SSE.
I recorded my laptop's TTFT and TPOT for a short prompt from the gateway log.
I saw ttfb from curl roughly match the gateway's ttftMs.
Closing curl early logs completion_cancelled and stops generation.
